newsitem.title: UK: Brazil weighs Brady buyback aided by global bond.
newsitem.headline: Brazil weighs Brady buyback aided by global bond.

text.p: Brazil said on Tuesday the possibility of a Brady bond buy-back remained high on its financial agenda and the launch this week of a dollar denominated global bond was a move in that direction.

"We see this as an interesting step to take at some point in the future," said Gustavo Franco, director of international affairs at Brazil's central bank, referring to moves by Mexico and the Philippines earlier this year to retire outstanding Brady bonds.
While this process was unlikely to be financed by any more new debt issues this year, he said Monday's issue of a five-year global bond was a move towards this end.

"It's not the first step, but it's one step in the sense that we've done deals before in the same type of maturity indicating more or less where the level where Brazil risk should be for new debt," he said.
"Possibly other new issues could help make this point in other maturities."

In London for the launch of the country's first dollar denominated bond since 1982 -- a $750 million global issue priced at 265 basis points over Treasuries, he said the paper had been sold chiefly to first-time retail investors.

"Sixty to 70 percent of the bond was sold to retail clients in Asia and Europe and more than half were first time buyers," he said, adding that they were more concerned with the big picture of Brazil's fundamentals than the daily news from Brazil. He denied the issue had been mis-priced after the deal widened to about 280 basis points over Treasuries in the secondary market late on Monday.
"When you do an aggressive sale of paper with an aggressive price it's common that you face difficulties in the three days after issue on the secondary market," he said.
"It's only natural for the issue to settle at par within a couple of days."

Brazil said it intended to use the bond to set a benchmark so its corporate issuers could follow it into the foreign capital markets. Selling the paper off cheaply would not help the private sector in the same way, he said. Investor memory of its 1980s debt crisis was one of the primary obstacles to its receiving a higher foreign currency debt rating.
Brazil's long term foreign currency debt is currently rated B1 by Moody's and B plus, with a positive outlook, by Standard & Poor's.
"For one of the rating agencies Brazil is still one or two notches below Argentina, Mexico and Russia," he said.

"But it is one thing what the agencies think and another what the market thinks -- market measurement of the relative risk between the three suggest Brazil is a country of less risk than the others, although it is exactly the opposite when you look at the rating agencies," he added.
But he added such memories should have a declining impact as time went on.
